questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of price skimming?
options: Setting a high price at launch, then lowering it as the market grows and rivals arrive
Setting a low price at launch to win market share quickly
Setting price below cost to force rivals out of the market
Adding a percentage mark-up to the unit cost
questions.why: Skimming starts high and comes down. The defining feature is the movement over time, not simply that the price is high.
whyNot: That is penetration pricing, which works in the opposite direction.
That is predatory pricing, which is illegal in many countries.
That is cost plus pricing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of penetration pricing?
options: Setting a low price on entering a market to win customers and share, then raising it later
Setting a high price to signal quality
Matching the prices charged by competitors
Pricing at $9.99 rather than $10
questions.why: Penetration buys share with a low launch price and raises it once customers are established. It needs deep pockets, because margins are thin or negative at first.
whyNot: That is skimming, or premium pricing.
That is competitive pricing.
That is psychological pricing.

questions.stem: Which pricing strategy is illegal in many countries?
options: Predatory pricing
Penetration pricing
Cost plus pricing
Psychological pricing
questions.why: Predatory pricing means selling below cost to destroy competitors, then raising prices once they have gone. It is treated as an abuse of market power. Never recommend it in an answer without saying so.
whyNot: Penetration pricing is a legal and common way to enter a market.
Cost plus is a standard and entirely legal method.
Psychological pricing is a normal, legal marketing tactic.

questions.stem: A product has a unit cost of $5.00 and the business applies a 40% mark-up. What is the cost plus price?
questions.why: Price = unit cost + (unit cost x mark-up) = 5.00 + (5.00 x 0.40) = 5.00 + 2.00 = $7.00.
whyNot: This adds 40 cents rather than 40% of $5.00. The mark-up is a percentage, not an amount.
That is the price for a 40% MARGIN, which is a percentage of the selling price. Mark-up is a percentage of cost.
That is the mark-up amount on its own. It still has to be added to the unit cost.

questions.stem: Total costs are $12,000 and 400 units are produced. What is the unit cost?
whyNot: This is ten times too small. 12,000 / 400 is 30, not 3.
This is ten times too large. Check the division.
This multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: Which factor most supports a business being able to charge a premium price?
options: A strong brand and genuine differentiation
A crowded market with many close substitutes
Highly price elastic demand
Customers who compare prices online easily
questions.why: Differentiation and brand strength give pricing freedom, because customers see fewer real alternatives and demand becomes less price elastic.
whyNot: Many substitutes means customers switch readily, which forces prices down.
Elastic demand means a price rise loses a lot of volume, so a premium is hard to sustain.
Easy comparison makes demand more elastic and squeezes prices.

questions.stem: What is the main weakness of cost plus pricing?
options: It ignores what customers are actually willing to pay
It never covers the cost of production
It is illegal in most markets
It cannot be calculated without knowing rival prices
questions.why: Cost plus works entirely from internal figures. If the resulting price is above what customers will pay you sell nothing; if it is below, you have given away margin.
whyNot: It guarantees a margin on every unit sold, provided the units sell. Covering cost is its strength.
It is a standard, legal method.
It needs no information about rivals at all, which is precisely the problem.

questions.stem: A hotel uses cost plus pricing. Occupancy falls, so fixed cost per room night rises. What happens, and why is it a problem?
options: The calculated price rises just when demand is weakest
The calculated price falls, attracting more customers
The mark-up percentage automatically falls
Variable cost per unit rises
questions.why: Fixed costs spread over fewer units means a higher unit cost, so the same mark-up produces a higher price. Cost plus therefore pushes prices up exactly when the market is soft, which is the opposite of what is needed. This is the strongest evaluation point on the strategy.
whyNot: Lower occupancy raises unit cost, which raises the cost plus price rather than lowering it.
The mark-up is a decision by the business. It does not change by itself.
Variable cost per unit is unchanged by occupancy; it is the fixed cost per unit that moves.

questions.stem: Which pricing strategy is most appropriate for a new, genuinely innovative technology product with no direct rivals?
options: Price skimming
Penetration pricing
Competitive pricing
Predatory pricing
questions.why: With no substitutes, early adopters will pay a premium, so a high launch price recovers development costs quickly and signals quality. The price then falls as competitors arrive.
whyNot: Penetration sacrifices margin to win share, which is wasteful when there is no competition to fight for share against.
There are no rivals to price against.
There is nobody to drive out, and it would be illegal in many markets anyway.

questions.stem: How have price comparison websites changed pricing in many markets?
options: Demand has become more price elastic, squeezing margins
Demand has become less price elastic
Businesses can now charge higher prices more easily
Cost plus pricing has become more accurate
questions.why: Customers can compare every seller in seconds at no cost, so more of them switch on price. That makes demand more elastic and pushes businesses towards competitive pricing.
whyNot: Easier comparison increases willingness to switch, which increases elasticity.
The opposite: comparison makes premium pricing harder unless the product is genuinely differentiated.
Comparison sites tell you nothing about your own costs, which is what cost plus uses.

questions.stem: What is the main risk of penetration pricing?
options: Thin or negative margins at the start, and customers anchored at the low price
That the business cannot attract any customers
That it is illegal in most countries
That it signals the product is high quality
questions.why: Penetration needs cash to fund the early low-margin period, and once customers are used to the low price, the planned increase loses some of them. It can also position the brand as cheap.
whyNot: Attracting customers is what it does well. The problem is what it costs to do so.
It is legal. Predatory pricing is the one to be careful about.
A low price signals the opposite, which is one of its drawbacks for a premium positioning.

questions.stem: In which stage of the product life cycle is competitive pricing most likely to dominate?
options: Maturity
Introduction
Development
Decline
questions.why: In maturity the market is saturated, differentiation has narrowed and rivals are established, so businesses price against each other to defend share.
whyNot: At introduction a differentiated product can skim, or a challenger can use penetration.
There are no sales in development, so no pricing decision yet.
In decline the usual approach is discounting to clear stock, or harvesting with minimal spend.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of psychological pricing?
options: Setting a price that appears lower than it is, such as $9.99 instead of $10
Setting price in line with competitors
Setting a high price to recover development costs
Adding a mark-up to unit cost
questions.why: Psychological pricing exploits how customers read prices. It genuinely affects perception, and it is a tactic layered on top of a strategy rather than a strategy itself.
whyNot: That is competitive pricing.
That is price skimming.
That is cost plus pricing.

questions.stem: A small business considers pricing below cost to drive out a larger rival. What is the best advice?
options: Do not: it is illegal in many countries and the larger rival can sustain losses far longer
Do it, because low prices always win market share
Do it, but only for one week
Do it and raise prices immediately afterwards
questions.why: Predatory pricing is both legally risky and strategically backwards here: the party with deeper reserves wins a war of losses, and that is the larger firm. A small business would run out of cash first.
whyNot: Winning share at a loss is only useful if you survive to raise prices, which a small firm probably would not.
A short period does not remove the legal exposure and would not force out a larger rival.
Raising prices straight after is exactly the pattern regulators look for.
